I'm going to give a contrarian take on Neoclouds like $NBIS and say the theme looks compelling after the valuation crash. 

Since there's a reason why Elon's $SPCX is heavily focused on this market full of "guppies" that would die: 

He sees how attractive the economics are after selling compute to $GOOGL and Anthropic. 

And this is reflected by his actions not words, from SpaceX's recent $40B financing for GPUs procurement. 
$AMZN, $MSFT, and even $META also see how profitable the economics are and are accelerating their AI DC buildouts. 

I'd argue if a Neocloud has: 

- Close relationships with $NVDA + others for allocations
- Existing contracted capacity + permitting
- Well funded counterparties, such as Hyperscalers. 
- Attractive economics, such as financing their procurement correctly (not the way $CRWV has with high debt interest unless they refinance). 

Then I think they'll do just fine... 

However, the bigger worry is more toward newer players starting financing or the permitting process, since barrier to entry has now become extremely high. 

For financing, read through on $IREN earnings has shown public Neoclouds can adapt extremely well to tight markets:

As seen with their 90% prepayments for GPU capex on a 5Y deal. 

Their older H100 GPUs recontracted at double their previous pricing and 12% higher contracted pricing also point against depreciation fears. 

And in the case DC buildouts slow from permitting delays... it heavily favors some over others. 

Rosenblatt's recent note for example stated they see little risk with $NBIS primary buildout that was in Missouri, Pennsylvania, and South Carolina. 

And there's probably less risk with developers in places like Australia. 

Markets have also show this infinite compute arbitrage can't go on forever, hence the reluctance to further finance capex, via things like ATMs. 

But ironically, tighter financing and hypothetical restrictive permitting would increase the competitive advantage of established neoclouds. 

And create a larger moat against newer DC developers.

Announcing a new Subscriber App: CLO Equity CEF Dashboard. Track the risks and rewards of Short Duration Equity Risk, one fund and one quarter at a time.

Unlike a bank, a CLO Equity tranche disgorges its earnings instead of retaining them, so most of the return arrives as cash early on rather than depending on a Greater Fool to pay up for a Terminal Value years from now. I laid out that framing on the Debt Serious podcast, walked through it question by question in CLO Equity CEF FAQ, Part I and Part II, and revisited it this summer in my conversation with ECC’s CFO.

I did not expect Spread Compression to punish the asset class as badly as it has. Tighter loan spreads against fixed CLO liabilities squeezed the Equity Arbitrage, distributions ran ahead of earnings, and then a wave of credit fear marked down CLO Equity without an actual underlying Credit crisis. By late October, these funds were trading at 40-50% discounts to NAVs that had already been discounted.

I still believe in the resilience of the asset class and its ability to distribute its way out. An individual CLO Equity tranche is designed to pay itself out over time, so NAV erosion is a feature rather than a bug, and the right way to judge it is Total Return, with distributions as the built-in Exit Strategy.

Conviction is not the same as monitoring, though. To know whether the thesis is holding, I need to see, fund by fund and quarter by quarter, whether income is covering the payout and how much of each NAV decline is a mark that can reverse versus value that is gone for good. No single source shows all of that side by side, so I built an analytical dashboard that tracks every metric I care about, and I have made it available to my paid subscribers.

Everyone who keeps sharing these short interest charts is missing the flows behind them. Most shops are not taking outright short bets. This is another effort to ease margin requirements across the street: banks providing balance sheet for more speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure.

The sequence on the street looks like this:

HF manager: “I want more margin.”

Bank: “Things look risky in public AI bets, and we’re already lending a lot against private AI bets. For some clients, we’ll extend more financing, but only if they add more short exposure to improve their collateral scores.”

HF manager: “Okay, I’ll short more stock against my main bet.”

That is how you end up with short exposures that look astronomically high while many end users remain heavily long tech. The additional shorts are supporting the financing of their main bets.

posts.name: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
The interesting thing about AI agents is that as a theoretical matter, their inference can kind of run anywhere. AI is one of the few areas of technology that isn’t *as* sensitive to latency back to the user. 

Long running agents are now going to be the norm, which means it’s ok to send off work to an AI factory somewhere and that work can essentially be largely done within that remote data center and a final result spit back to the user. The data can pass into these systems in an encrypted manner, be combed through by agents, and then disregarded right after. 

And because the economic value of the task is so high relative to the latency sensitivity (eg getting back $500 in value from an automated task, but it takes an extra second to return), you don’t have to have the inference to be particularly close to the user. 

Also, because inference is a temporary process with no sensitive data needing to be stored long term where the inference is happening, you can effectively treat AI factories as ephemeral systems, changing some of the data residency dynamics slightly.

Combined, this means you have more flexibility in where you can begin to deploy AI data centers. This is both a huge economic opportunity for the states or countries (or space) that want to take advantage of this fact. And it’s a loss to the states or countries that decide to forgo the opportunity.
